title: Renderings (Python)
text:
Python cells with renderings: [light, dark], which draw one plot for each color mode, as Renderings (R) does for R cells. The page shows the one for its mode (the toggle in the navbar), and so does the viewer. Each one is worth opening in light and dark mode.
Each case shows its source above the plot: Jupyter leaves panzoom: out of the echoed code of a cell.
The plots are drawn with this helper:
```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
```
wave()
```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "wave()"

def wave(k=1, ink="black", paper="white", col="#3B7DB8"):
    """Draw a sine wave with shading to zero.

    k: frequency multiplier; draws 2 * k cycles from 0 to 4 * pi.
    ink: color for the axes, labels, and title.
    paper: plot background color, or "none" for transparency.
    col: color for the curve and its shaded area.
    """
    x = np.linspace(0, 4 * np.pi, 400)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
    fig.patch.set_facecolor(paper)
    ax.set_facecolor(paper)
    ax.fill_between(x, np.sin(k * x), color=col, alpha=0.35, linewidth=0)
    ax.plot(x, np.sin(k * x), color=col, linewidth=2)
    ax.set(title=f"Wave {k}", xlabel="x", ylabel="sin(kx)")
    ax.title.set_color(ink)
    ax.xaxis.label.set_color(ink)
    ax.yaxis.label.set_color(ink)
    ax.tick_params(colors=ink)
    for spine in ax.spines.values():
        spine.set_color(ink)
    plt.show()
```

title: Dark plots (R)
text:
Plots with dark backgrounds and plots with transparent backgrounds with the viewer’s default 70% black backdrop. Each one is worth opening in light and dark mode (the toggle in the navbar). Renderings draws a plot for each mode instead.
The site draws R plots on white (dev.args: bg: white in _quarto.yml), so the transparent plots set bg = "transparent" in their own cells. They use the ragg_png device, since R’s own png device tints light text drawn on a transparent background.
The plots are drawn with this helper:
wave()
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "wave()"

#' Draw a sine wave with shading to zero.
#'
#' @param k Frequency multiplier; the curve completes 2 * k cycles on 0 to 4 * pi.
#' @param ink Color for the axes, labels, and title.
#' @param paper Plot background color, or NULL to keep the device background.
#' @param col Color for the curve and its shaded area.
wave <- function(k = 1, ink = "black", paper = NULL, col = "#3B7DB8") {
  if (!is.null(paper)) {
    par(bg = paper)
  }
  par(fg = ink, col.axis = ink, col.lab = ink, col.main = ink)
  x <- seq(0, 4 * pi, length.out = 400)
  plot(
    x,
    sin(k * x),
    type = "n",
    main = paste("Wave", k),
    xlab = "x",
    ylab = "sin(kx)"
  )
  polygon(
    c(x, rev(x)),
    c(sin(k * x), rep(0, length(x))),
    col = adjustcolor(col, 0.35),
    border = NA
  )
  lines(x, sin(k * x), lwd = 2, col = col)
}
```

title: Divs (R)
text:
Figures inside the divs built into Quarto: callouts, tabsets, page columns, and conditional content, each on its own and inside a .panzoom div. lightbox is off, so clicking an image panzoom leaves alone does nothing.
An image on a tab not selected, or in a collapsed callout, opens once the reader selects the tab or expands the callout.
The plots are drawn with these helpers:
collage()
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "collage()"

#' Draw random walks in side-by-side panels.
#'
#' @param n Number of panels.
collage <- function(n = 12) {
  set.seed(1)
  par(mfrow = c(1, n), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 1))
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    plot(
      cumsum(rnorm(200)),
      type = "l",
      main = paste("Panel", i),
      xlab = "",
      ylab = "",
      col = hcl.colors(n)[i],
      lwd = 2
    )
  }
}
```
wave()
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "wave()"

#' Draw a sine wave with shading to zero.
#'
#' @param k Frequency multiplier; the curve completes 2 * k cycles on 0 to 4 * pi.
wave <- function(k = 1) {
  x <- seq(0, 4 * pi, length.out = 400)
  col <- hcl.colors(4, "Dark 3")[(k - 1) %% 4 + 1]
  plot(
    x,
    sin(k * x),
    type = "n",
    main = paste("Wave", k),
    xlab = "x",
    ylab = "sin(kx)"
  )
  polygon(
    c(x, rev(x)),
    c(sin(k * x), rep(0, length(x))),
    col = adjustcolor(col, 0.35),
    border = NA
  )
  lines(x, sin(k * x), lwd = 2, col = col)
}
```

text:
The cell options from the R examples, on matplotlib figures, and svg output. lightbox is not set in the YAML header, so only cells marked for panzoom open in it. Clicking any other figure does nothing, unless its cell turns lightbox on with #| lightbox: true. This notebook’s YAML header adds the panzoom filter:
Jupyter leaves the panzoom and lightbox options out of the code shown on the page, unlike knitr. The Code button at the top shows the full source.
The plots share this setup and helper:
```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
```
walk()
```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "walk()"

def walk(ax, n=200, title=None):
    """Draw a random walk using the shared random number generator.

    ax: matplotlib axes to draw on.
    n: number of steps.
    title: optional axes title.
    """
    ax.plot(np.cumsum(rng.normal(size=n)))
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title)
```

title: Wide and tall figures (R)
text:
Figures of different shapes, each opened on its own, and the fit option. All are png. Other formats are on image formats, and the same shapes in galleries and layouts are on wide figures in galleries.
With fit: auto, the default, a figure opens by its shape:
fit: contain, height, or width sets this for one figure. A small image opens at its own size, and scrolling still zooms it in, up to max-zoom.
Where you click a strip on the page is its focal point: the viewer opens with that spot in the middle of the screen. Near either end of the strip, that end lines up with the edge of the screen instead. The 0 key and double-click return to it. Opened from the keyboard, a strip starts at its left end or top. Zooming out still shows the whole figure.
Shift+scroll, or a sideways trackpad swipe, pans sideways, and Alt+scroll pans up and down.
The plots are drawn with these helpers:
collage()
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "collage()"

#' Draw random walks in side-by-side panels.
#'
#' @param n Number of panels.
collage <- function(n = 12) {
  set.seed(1)
  par(mfrow = c(1, n), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 1))
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    plot(
      cumsum(rnorm(200)),
      type = "l",
      main = paste("Panel", i),
      xlab = "",
      ylab = "",
      col = hcl.colors(n)[i],
      lwd = 2
    )
  }
}
```
strip()
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "strip()"

#' Draw random walks in stacked rows.
#'
#' Each seed selects a palette, omitting its lightest colors.
#'
#' @param seed Random seed and palette selector.
#' @param n Number of rows.
strip <- function(seed = 2, n = 8) {
  set.seed(seed)
  palette <- c(
    "Viridis",
    "Plasma",
    "Zissou 1",
    "Dark 3",
    "Sunset",
    "Cividis",
    "Dynamic",
    "Inferno"
  )[(seed - 2) %% 8 + 1]
  par(mfrow = c(n, 1), mar = c(2, 3, 2, 1))
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    plot(
      cumsum(rnorm(100)),
      type = "l",
      main = paste0("Strip ", seed, ", row ", i),
      xlab = "",
      ylab = "",
      col = hcl.colors(n + 2, palette)[i],
      lwd = 2
    )
  }
}
```
wave()
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "wave()"

#' Draw a sine wave with shading to zero.
#'
#' @param k Frequency multiplier; the curve completes 2 * k cycles on 0 to 4 * pi.
wave <- function(k = 1) {
  x <- seq(0, 4 * pi, length.out = 400)
  col <- hcl.colors(4, "Dark 3")[(k - 1) %% 4 + 1]
  plot(
    x,
    sin(k * x),
    type = "n",
    main = paste("Wave", k),
    xlab = "x",
    ylab = "sin(kx)"
  )
  polygon(
    c(x, rev(x)),
    c(sin(k * x), rep(0, length(x))),
    col = adjustcolor(col, 0.35),
    border = NA
  )
  lines(x, sin(k * x), lwd = 2, col = col)
}
```

title: Reference
text: Enable the extension with filters: [panzoom]. Set options under panzoom: in the document header, under #| panzoom: in a code cell, or as attributes on a selected markdown image. Cell and image options override document options.

title: Reference
text:
Selecting images







Setting
Applies to




panzoom: true or panzoom: auto
Every figure and every image alone in its paragraph.


panzoom: false
No images in the document, including explicitly selected images.


panzoom: with an option map
Selected images only, unless the map includes match: auto.


#| panzoom: true
All plots from that code cell. A cell option map also selects its plots.


.panzoom on an image or div
That image, or every image inside the div.


.nopanzoom on an image, or #| panzoom: false on a cell
Excludes the image or cell’s plots.



See selecting images and divs for examples.

title: Reference
text:
Viewer options
“Document” means the document’s panzoom: map; “cell/image” means a cell’s #| panzoom: map or an attribute on a markdown image.



Option
Default
Scope
Description




match
Selected images
Document
Set to auto to select every figure and standalone image.


max-zoom
4
Document, cell/image
Maximum screen pixels per image pixel.


hint
true
Document, cell/image
true or show shows the controls hint; hide starts hidden but allows toggling; false removes it. Opening by touch hides the hint initially.


caption
true
Document, cell/image
Show the figure caption in the viewer.


loop
false
Document
Wrap from the last gallery image to the first, and back.


fit
auto
Document, cell/image
auto, contain, height, or width; see below.


desc-position
Figure caption position
Document, cell/image
Place the caption and description at bottom, top, left, or right. Side panels move below the image on screens narrower than 769 px.


css-class
None
Document, cell/image
Add a class to the viewer for custom CSS.


keys
See Keyboard options
Document
Change keys for viewer actions.


group
Automatic for subfigures
Cell/image
Give images the same group name to form a gallery. Also supported on .panzoom divs.


description
None
Cell/image
Markdown text below the caption. A cell can use a list with one description per plot, in order.



With fit: auto, most images open whole, never larger than their real size. Very wide images open at screen height, near the clicked spot; very tall images open at screen width, from the top. Choose contain to always open the whole image, or height or width to force the corresponding fit.
See cell options, captions and descriptions, and wide and tall figures.

Document example
---
filters:
  - panzoom
panzoom:
  match: auto
  max-zoom: 6
  loop: true
  desc-position: bottom
---


Cell and image examples
```{r}

#|   max-zoom: 8
#|   hint: false
#|   group: pressure
#|   description:
#|     - "Pressure against temperature."
#|     - "The same, on a log scale."

plot(pressure)
plot(pressure, log = "y")
```

title: Reference
text:
Keyboard options
Set keys in the document’s panzoom: map. Each action accepts one key, a list of keys, or false to disable its binding. Omitted actions keep their defaults.



Action
Default
Behavior




caption
c
Hide or show the caption and description.


hint
h
Hide or show the hint.


close
Escape
Close the viewer.


reset
"0"
Return to the opening view.


zoom-in
["+", "="]
Zoom in.


zoom-out
"-"
Zoom out.



panzoom:
  keys:
    caption: k
    hint: false
    close: [Escape, q]
A key is one character, or Escape, Backspace, Delete, or Insert. Each key can serve only one action. Tab, Enter, Space, arrow keys, Page Up, Page Down, Home, and End have fixed behavior. Left and Right change gallery images; Ctrl/Cmd+arrow pans when the image is larger than the screen.

title: panzoom
text:
Wide figure
A figure many times wider than tall would be too thin to read if it opened whole, so it opens at screen height, at the spot you clicked. panzoom does this on its own for very wide figures; here, fit: height is set so this figure always opens that way, whatever the window’s shape. Click the highlighted panel, and the viewer opens right on it.

```{r}
#| panzoom:
#|   fit: height
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Eight line plots of random walks side by side; the sixth, titled Click
#|   here, is highlighted in yellow and pink
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Eight simulated random walks of 200 steps each, with the sixth highlighted.

set.seed(1)
par(mfrow = c(1, 8), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 1), cex.main = 1.3)
for (i in 1:8) {
  y <- cumsum(rnorm(200))
  if (i == 6) {
    plot(y, type = "n", main = "Click here", col.main = "#c2185b")
    usr <- par("usr")
    rect(usr[1], usr[3], usr[2], usr[4], col = "#fff3b0", border = NA)
    lines(y, col = "#c2185b", lwd = 3)
  } else {
    plot(y, type = "l", main = paste("Panel", i))
  }
}
```




Eight simulated random walks of 200 steps each, with the sixth highlighted.

text:
Math and code in captions
Captions and descriptions keep their math and inline code, typeset as on the page, along with citations, cross-references, and links.

```{r}
#| panzoom:
#|   description: >-
#|     $\varphi(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-x^2/2}$, drawn with `dnorm(x)`.
#|     The shaded area is $P(|X| < 1) \approx 0.683$.
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   The bell curve of the standard normal density, with the area between -1 and
#|   1 shaded grey
#| fig-cap: "The standard normal density, $\\varphi(x)$."

x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 400)
plot(x, dnorm(x), type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "x", ylab = "density")
inner <- abs(x) < 1
polygon(
  c(-1, x[inner], 1),
  c(0, dnorm(x[inner]), 0),
  col = "grey85",
  border = NA
)
lines(x, dnorm(x), lwd = 2)
```




The standard normal density, \(\varphi(x)\).





\(\varphi(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-x^2/2}\), drawn with dnorm(x). The shaded area is \(P(|X| < 1) \approx 0.683\).

title: Image formats (R)
text:
Two figures, a wide collage and a standard plot, written by different knitr graphics devices: webp, svg, png, pdf, and an animated gif. Every figure has the #| panzoom: true cell option and opens in panzoom unless its case says otherwise. How figures of other shapes open is on wide and tall figures.
knitr has no built-in webp device, so the webp cases use agg_webp from ragg. knitr passes it sizes in inches and no resolution, while ragg expects pixels and draws at 72 dpi, so each webp case sets both under dev.args:
res: 96 gives the webp the same size as the other figures on the page.
The collage cases draw with this helper:
```{r}
library(ragg)
```
collage()
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "collage()"

#' Draw random walks in side-by-side panels.
#'
#' @param n Number of panels.
collage <- function(n = 12) {
  set.seed(1)
  par(mfrow = c(1, n), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 1))
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    plot(
      cumsum(rnorm(200)),
      type = "l",
      main = paste("Panel", i),
      xlab = "",
      ylab = "",
      col = hcl.colors(n)[i],
      lwd = 2
    )
  }
}
```

title: Captions and descriptions (R)
text:
A caption is copied from the page, so whatever Quarto renders there comes through to the viewer. A description is rendered with the page too, in a hidden block the viewer copies, so its citations resolve, its cross-references get numbers, and a work cited only in a description is still listed under References. In a caption, lightbox shows a citation as raw [@key].
The plots are drawn with this helper:
wave()
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "wave()"

#' Draw a sine wave with shading to zero.
#'
#' @param k Frequency multiplier; the curve completes 2 * k cycles on 0 to 4 * pi.
wave <- function(k = 1) {
  x <- seq(0, 4 * pi, length.out = 400)
  col <- hcl.colors(4, "Dark 3")[(k - 1) %% 4 + 1]
  plot(
    x,
    sin(k * x),
    type = "n",
    main = paste("Wave", k),
    xlab = "x",
    ylab = "sin(kx)"
  )
  polygon(
    c(x, rev(x)),
    c(sin(k * x), rep(0, length(x))),
    col = adjustcolor(col, 0.35),
    border = NA
  )
  lines(x, sin(k * x), lwd = 2, col = col)
}
```

title: Wide figures in galleries (R)
text:
Collages (25 × 2 inches) and tall strips in galleries, as subfigures, and in a layout div. The same shapes on their own, and the fit option, are on wide and tall figures.
Wide figures open at screen height, and tall ones at screen width. The one you click opens at the spot you clicked, and stepping to another in a gallery starts it at its left end or top. The left and right arrow keys always step through the gallery, the same as the previous and next buttons; Ctrl/Cmd+arrow pans a wide figure instead, in any direction, without changing image. The viewer keeps the sides of the screen free for the previous and next buttons, so a figure shown whole, or panned to its end, is never under one.
The plots are drawn with these helpers:
collage()
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "collage()"

#' Draw random walks in side-by-side panels.
#'
#' @param n Number of panels.
collage <- function(n = 12) {
  set.seed(1)
  par(mfrow = c(1, n), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 1))
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    plot(
      cumsum(rnorm(200)),
      type = "l",
      main = paste("Panel", i),
      xlab = "",
      ylab = "",
      col = hcl.colors(n)[i],
      lwd = 2
    )
  }
}
```
strip()
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "strip()"

#' Draw random walks in stacked rows.
#'
#' Each seed selects a palette, omitting its lightest colors.
#'
#' @param seed Random seed and palette selector.
#' @param n Number of rows.
strip <- function(seed = 2, n = 8) {
  set.seed(seed)
  palette <- c(
    "Viridis",
    "Plasma",
    "Zissou 1",
    "Dark 3",
    "Sunset",
    "Cividis",
    "Dynamic",
    "Inferno"
  )[(seed - 2) %% 8 + 1]
  par(mfrow = c(n, 1), mar = c(2, 3, 2, 1))
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    plot(
      cumsum(rnorm(100)),
      type = "l",
      main = paste0("Strip ", seed, ", row ", i),
      xlab = "",
      ylab = "",
      col = hcl.colors(n + 2, palette)[i],
      lwd = 2
    )
  }
}
```

title: Captions, formats, and shapes (Python)
text:
This page repeats the R cell-options, caption, format, and shape cases on matplotlib figures. The YAML header sets loop, so the looping gallery wraps around.
Jupyter figures are shown at their size in inches × 96 px, and written at twice that, so a figure here opens at up to twice its size on the page. Quarto gives each figure that width, so one wider than about 8 inches runs past the column. The collages here are at most 8 inches wide, where the R pages use 25.
The plots are drawn with these helpers:
```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
```
wave()
```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "wave()"

def wave(k=1):
    """Draw a sine wave with shading to zero.

    k: frequency multiplier; draws 2 * k cycles from 0 to 4 * pi.
    """
    x = np.linspace(0, 4 * np.pi, 400)
    col = plt.cm.Dark2(k - 1)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
    ax.fill_between(x, np.sin(k * x), color=col, alpha=0.35, linewidth=0)
    ax.plot(x, np.sin(k * x), color=col, linewidth=2)
    ax.set(title=f"Wave {k}", xlabel="x", ylabel="sin(kx)")
    plt.show()
```
collage()
```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "collage()"

def collage(n=12, height=0.8, width=8):
    """Draw random walks in side-by-side panels.

    n: number of panels.
    height: figure height in inches.
    width: figure width in inches.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, n, figsize=(width, height), layout="constrained")
    for i, ax in enumerate(axes):
        ax.plot(np.cumsum(rng.normal(size=200)), color=plt.cm.viridis(i / n))
        ax.set_title(f"Panel {i + 1}", fontsize=5)
        ax.tick_params(labelsize=4)
    plt.show()
```
strip()
```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "strip()"

def strip(seed=2, n=8):
    """Draw random walks in stacked rows.

    seed: random seed for the walks.
    n: number of rows.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(n, 1, figsize=(3, 10), layout="constrained")
    for i, ax in enumerate(axes):
        ax.plot(np.cumsum(rng.normal(size=100)), color=plt.cm.plasma(i / n))
```

text:
7 Long description
A cell with a description longer than its panel, under the panzoom cell option. It opens in panzoom, and the description panel scrolls. Tab reaches the panel, and the arrow keys, Page Up and Page Down, Home, End, and Space scroll it.

```{python}
#| fig-alt: A sine curve, shaded between the curve and y = 0
#| fig-cap: |-
#| 
#|   Wave 1: y = sin(x); the area between the curve and y = 0 is shaded.

wave(1)
```




Wave 1: y = sin(x); the area between the curve and y = 0 is shaded.





This description is long on purpose: it is taller than the space the viewer gives a description, so its panel scrolls. With a mouse or trackpad, scrolling over the panel scrolls it. From the keyboard, Tab moves focus to the panel, and then the arrow keys, Page Up and Page Down, Home, End and Space scroll it, as they would scroll a page. The image stays where it is meanwhile, and the page behind the viewer doesn’t move. Tab again moves on to the close button, and Esc still closes the viewer. Plots like this one often come with long notes: what was measured, how, and over what range; what the axes mean; what to look for and what to ignore. Notes like these can run to several paragraphs, and a reader who uses the keyboard must be able to read all of them, not just the lines that fit. In a short window, or on a phone, the panel is smaller still, so even a description of two or three sentences can scroll there. The panel is a Tab stop only while it scrolls, so a short description adds no extra stop. The rest of this description only adds length, so that it scrolls in every window the tests use, including the wide screen, where the panel is tallest and its lines are longest. The wave rises from zero to one over the first quarter of each period, falls back to zero at the half period, reaches minus one at three quarters, and returns to zero at the end of the period. The shaded area above the axis equals the shaded area below it over each whole period, so the mean of the wave is zero. Doubling k halves the period and doubles the number of crossings, and the shading follows the curve wherever it goes. The curve is drawn with 400 points, enough that it looks smooth at any zoom the viewer allows. Its color comes from the Dark2 palette, one color per wave, and its shading is the same color at a third of the strength, so the curve stays the strongest line in the plot. The title names the wave, the x axis runs over two whole periods, and the y axis is labeled with the formula the curve follows. Each of these choices is made once, in the helper, so every wave on this page is drawn the same way and only k changes. Nothing in this description is needed for the test except its length: a description this long scrolls in any window.

Python cells inside the divs built into Quarto: callouts, tabsets, and page columns, each on its own and inside a .panzoom div, as Divs (R) does for R cells and images. lightbox is off, so clicking a plot panzoom leaves alone does nothing.
A plot on a tab not selected, or in a collapsed callout, opens once the reader selects the tab or expands the callout.
Each case shows its source above the plot: Jupyter leaves panzoom: out of the echoed code of a cell.
The plots are drawn with these helpers:
```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
```
wave()
```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "wave()"

def wave(k=1):
    """Draw a sine wave with shading to zero.

    k: frequency multiplier; draws 2 * k cycles from 0 to 4 * pi.
    """
    x = np.linspace(0, 4 * np.pi, 400)
    col = plt.cm.Dark2(k - 1)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
    ax.fill_between(x, np.sin(k * x), color=col, alpha=0.35, linewidth=0)
    ax.plot(x, np.sin(k * x), color=col, linewidth=2)
    ax.set(title=f"Wave {k}", xlabel="x", ylabel="sin(kx)")
    plt.show()
```
collage()
```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "collage()"

def collage(n=12, height=0.8, width=8):
    """Draw random walks in side-by-side panels.

    n: number of panels.
    height: figure height in inches.
    width: figure width in inches.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, n, figsize=(width, height), layout="constrained")
    for i, ax in enumerate(axes):
        ax.plot(np.cumsum(rng.normal(size=200)), color=plt.cm.viridis(i / n))
        ax.set_title(f"Panel {i + 1}", fontsize=5)
        ax.tick_params(labelsize=4)
    plt.show()
```

title: Renderings (R)
text:
R cells with renderings: [light, dark], which draw one plot for each color mode. The page shows the one for its mode (the toggle in the navbar), and so does the viewer. Each one is worth opening in light and dark mode.
The transparent plots use the ragg_png device, since the base R png device tints light text drawn on a transparent background.
The plots are drawn with this helper:
wave()
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "wave()"

#' Draw a sine wave with shading to zero.
#'
#' @param k Frequency multiplier; the curve completes 2 * k cycles on 0 to 4 * pi.
#' @param ink Color for the axes, labels, and title.
#' @param paper Plot background color, or NULL to keep the device background.
#' @param col Color for the curve and its shaded area.
wave <- function(k = 1, ink = "black", paper = NULL, col = "#3B7DB8") {
  if (!is.null(paper)) {
    par(bg = paper)
  }
  par(fg = ink, col.axis = ink, col.lab = ink, col.main = ink)
  x <- seq(0, 4 * pi, length.out = 400)
  plot(
    x,
    sin(k * x),
    type = "n",
    main = paste("Wave", k),
    xlab = "x",
    ylab = "sin(kx)"
  )
  polygon(
    c(x, rev(x)),
    c(sin(k * x), rep(0, length(x))),
    col = adjustcolor(col, 0.35),
    border = NA
  )
  lines(x, sin(k * x), lwd = 2, col = col)
}
```
